clue.text: Judge has trouble with home getting cooler

parts.note: J is the standard abbreviation for judge
to ail is to be troubled or unwell
a house is a home; 'with' just joins it on

explanation.surface: A judge struggles with a house that keeps getting colder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooler' looks like a comparative about temperature, but it is slang for a prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Cooler is old slang for a prison, and a jailhouse is likewise a prison building.

clue.text: Card player's first to put up stakes

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting something up lifts it so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: the jack is a playing card

indicators.note: the first of a word means only its opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of player
the word to, turned upwards

explanation.surface: A card player is first to put up money for the bets.
explanation.definitionFit: The jackpot is the pool of accumulated stakes in a game, won all at once.

clue.text: See 16
Trim dealer?

parts.note: surface reading: someone who deals in trimming, as a barber trims hair
setter's reading: a seller of trimmings, the ribbons, buttons and braid that trim clothes

explanation.walkthrough: This is paired with 13-down, which has the same clue; here trim is a noun for decorative sewing goods, not a haircut.
explanation.definitionFit: A haberdasher is a shopkeeper selling sewing notions such as ribbon, lace and buttons, all classed as trimmings.

clue.text: Returning letter to Athens, attache died alone

indicators.note: something returning goes back the way it came, so the letter's name is read backwards

parts.note: nu is a Greek letter, a letter to an Athenian; turned back it reads un
an attaché is a diplomatic aide
D is the abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: Returning a letter to Athens, a diplomat died on their own.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something alone means doing it without help from anyone.

clue.text: No longer active, one-time Conservative's put in shade

parts.note: ex- means former

indicators.note: being put in something means being placed inside it

parts.note: a tint is a shade of colour
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: A former Tory politician, no longer active, has been overshadowed by rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s reads as 'is': the party letter is put inside the colour word, which follows the former prefix.
explanation.definitionFit: A volcano that is extinct will never erupt again, so it is permanently inactive.

clue.text: Pour the last of delicious cordial

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter only

parts.note: the final letter of delicious
a cordial welcome is a warm one

explanation.surface: An instruction to serve the final drops of a tasty fruit cordial.
explanation.walkthrough: Cordial looks like a drink but is the adjective meaning friendly.
explanation.definitionFit: Crowds pour or swarm into a place when they arrive in great numbers.

clue.text: Second-in-command making no mistake here

parts.note: the initials of the three words of this phrase

explanation.surface: A deputy who never slips up.
explanation.walkthrough: The initials of the hyphenated phrase spell the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sic is printed after a quoted error to show it is reproduced faithfully, meaning the slip was intended or original.

clue.text: Friendly stroll, skirting northbound main road

indicators.note: in a down clue, travelling north means reading upwards
to skirt something is to go round its edges

parts.note: to amble is to stroll
the A1 is Britain's main north-south road; going north it reads 1A, with the 1 as I

explanation.surface: A pleasant walk alongside the A1 heading north.
explanation.walkthrough: The A1 is the longest numbered road in Britain, running from London to Edinburgh.
explanation.definitionFit: An amiable person is friendly, good-natured and pleasant company.

clue.text: Isn't sure to clout conservationists

parts.note: clout and might both mean power
NT is the National Trust, the British conservation charity

explanation.surface: Uncertain whether to strike some environmental campaigners.
explanation.walkthrough: Clout looks like a verb meaning hit, but here it is the noun for influence.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something mightn't happen expresses doubt, so the contraction conveys being unsure.

clue.text: Cancel e-book about A-lister

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a run of letters straddling the two words, read in clue order

explanation.surface: Someone cancels an electronic book written about a famous person.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits backwards across the join of cancel and e-book.
explanation.definitionFit: A-listers are top-tier stars, and celeb is short for celebrity.

clue.text: Retired dude cheers sovereign for beginning vigorously

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing backwards, so the words that follow are read in reverse

parts.note: cat is jazz slang for a cool dude
ta is British informal thanks
a king is a sovereign

explanation.surface: A retired man raises a toast to the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Both of the first two words go backwards together, then the monarch follows unreversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Attacking a task means tackling it with energy from the start.

clue.text: Dash back for fix

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the word reads right to left

parts.note: to nip somewhere is to dash there briefly

explanation.surface: Hurry back to get something mended.
explanation.definitionFit: To pin something is to fasten or fix it in place.

clue.text: Spooner's concealing bunny in equestrian clothing

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so two words here trade their starts

parts.note: concealing is hiding and a bunny is a rabbit; swapping the opening sounds of that pair gives the outfit

explanation.surface: Someone hides a pet rabbit inside their riding outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of HIDING RABBIT and you get the outfit.
explanation.definitionFit: A riding habit is the traditional outfit, especially a woman's, worn on horseback.

clue.text: Trim dealer?

parts.note: surface reading: a trader in trims, the same words as 3-down's clue
setter's reading: a person whose trade is trimming people's hair

explanation.walkthrough: The twin of 3-down: here trim is a haircut, and the dealer deals them out to customers.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who cuts and styles hair offers a trim as a standard service in the salon.

clue.text: Wax modeller needing uniform as dust resettles

indicators.note: when something resettles it lands in a new arrangement

parts.note: U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sculptor of waxworks needs a uniform as the dust settles again.
explanation.walkthrough: Madame Tussaud founded the London waxworks museum that bears her name.
explanation.definitionFit: Marie Tussaud was a famous sculptor of wax figures, so she is the wax modeller.

clue.text: Verbally challenge cult to part on equal terms

indicators.note: verbally means spoken, so the words are heard rather than read

parts.note: to try is to put to the test; a sect is a cult

explanation.surface: Openly contest a religious cult so it splits fairly.
explanation.definitionFit: To trisect something is to divide it into three equal parts.

clue.text: Papers regularly restricting long letters

indicators.note: restricting something means hemming it in on both sides
regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of papers
to long for something is to itch for it

explanation.surface: Newspapers routinely limiting lengthy correspondence.
explanation.walkthrough: Long is a verb meaning yearn, not an adjective describing letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An aitch is the name of the letter H, so the plural names a set of such letters.

clue.text: Wild animals and sand in offshore Indian territories

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so the letters run riot into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Wild animals and sand are found on some islands off India.
explanation.definitionFit: The Andaman Islands are an archipelago in the Bay of Bengal that form part of an Indian union territory.

clue.text: More neglected stats uncovered by bank

indicators.note: uncovering something strips off its outer layer, so the end letters go

parts.note: stats with its first and last letters removed
a bank of seats is a tier

explanation.surface: Statistics revealed by a bank showing greater neglect.
explanation.definitionFit: Tatty means shabby and worn, the state of something neglected, and this is its comparative.

clue.text: Tolerate corporation

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to put up with
second meaning: corporation is jocular slang for a large belly

explanation.walkthrough: Corporation looks like a company, but it is old humorous slang for a paunch.
explanation.definitionFit: One can stomach an insult, and a big stomach was jokingly called a corporation.

clue.text: Base, base hound

parts.note: a bed is a base or foundation
base as an adjective means morally low

explanation.surface: A list that reads like a description of a lowly dog.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated word takes two senses: a foundation, then wickedness. Hound looks like a dog but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To bedevil someone is to harass or torment them persistently, as does hounding.

clue.text: Courage of unknown vicar shown up after booby trap

parts.note: a playful description of a bra, which holds the bust

indicators.note: in a down clue, showing something up raises it so it reads bottom to top

parts.note: y is a mathematical unknown
Rev is the title of a vicar, short for Reverend

explanation.surface: A vicar shows nerve by being exposed after setting off a hidden trap.
explanation.walkthrough: The unknown and the vicar go up together, so they come after the opening piece reading upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Bravery and courage are synonyms for facing danger without fear.

clue.text: Foul and sticky leaving South Carolina for Channel Isles

indicators.note: leaving one thing for another means swapping it out

parts.note: a viscous liquid is thick and sticky
SC is the postal abbreviation for South Carolina
CI is the abbreviation for the Channel Islands

explanation.surface: A nasty, sticky substance leaves South Carolina bound for the Channel Islands.
explanation.walkthrough: The Channel Islands are the British islands off Normandy, such as Jersey and Guernsey.
explanation.definitionFit: Vicious and foul both describe nasty, savage behaviour.

clue.text: Release this song from Disney film

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to set something free
second meaning: the hit song from Frozen

explanation.walkthrough: The Disney film is Frozen, whose best-known song is an anthem about releasing your feelings.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means relinquish hold of something, and is also the title of Elsa's ballad in Frozen.

clue.text: Check current fee to guard outlaws' leader and decline

indicators.note: a guard stands round what it protects, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: to deter is to check or prevent
I is the physics symbol for electric current

indicators.note: 'leader' keeps only the first letter of "outlaws'"

parts.note: the leading letter of outlaws
a rate is a fee or charge

explanation.surface: Curb rising charges to protect the gang boss, and fall away.
explanation.walkthrough: The current symbol and the fee together guard the outlaw letter: I(O)RATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To deteriorate is to get worse, which is to decline.

clue.text: Ignore wound

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a gash in the skin

explanation.walkthrough: Wound might be read as the past of wind, but it is the noun for an injury.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut someone dead is to snub them deliberately, and a cut is also a small injury.

clue.text: Principal set up computer

parts.note: principal means main
to frame someone is to set them up

explanation.surface: A head teacher is falsely set up by someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A mainframe is a large, powerful central computer serving many users.

clue.text: Oliver's principal ironclad opponent

indicators.note: something clad is wrapped in a covering, here the metal symbol

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

indicators.note: the principal part of a word is its head, its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of Oliver

explanation.surface: Oliver Cromwell's main enemy, armoured in iron.
explanation.walkthrough: The armour-plated look of ironclad hides the split: iron supplies the symbol and clad wraps it round.
explanation.definitionFit: A foe is an enemy or adversary, an opponent.

clue.text: Play to see, with Rex in it

indicators.note: having something in it means one element sits inside the other

parts.note: to spot is to see
R stands for Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A theatre play worth seeing, starring someone called Rex.
explanation.walkthrough: Play looks like a drama, but it means fun or games.
explanation.definitionFit: Sport and play both mean recreation or fun, as in done in sport.

clue.text: Body part on no account moving right forward

indicators.note: moving something forward lifts it from its place and sets it earlier in the word

parts.note: never means on no account
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A section of the body that must never be moved right forward.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the last letter out of the word for not ever and slot it in two places earlier.
explanation.definitionFit: A nerve is a fibre carrying signals through the body, so it is a body part.

clue.text: Triumphant declaration bemused Tory sheep

indicators.note: someone bemused is confused, so the letters are muddled up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Puzzled Conservative followers make a victorious announcement.
explanation.definitionFit: A conjuror says the exclamation at the moment of a trick's success, a cry of triumph.
